question_text: The Arabic term 'Tawhid' refers to the Islamic concept of:
option_a: The oneness and uniqueness of Allah
explanation: Tawhid is the fundamental Islamic belief in the absolute oneness of Allah, affirming that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.

question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the five pillars of Islam?
explanation: The five pillars are Shahadah, Salah, Zakat, Sawm (fasting), and Hajj. Jihad is an important concept but not counted among the five pillars.

question_text: The Shahadah, the declaration of faith in Islam, states that:
option_a: There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger
option_b: Allah is the creator of all things
option_c: Muhammad is the son of Allah
option_d: Prayer is the key to paradise
explanation: The Shahadah 'La ilaha illa Allah, Muhammadun Rasul Allah' is the foundational testimony of Islamic faith, affirming Allah's oneness and Muhammad's prophethood.

question_text: The concept of 'Risalah' in Islam refers to:
option_a: Prophethood and the message of Allah
explanation: Risalah means prophethood or the message delivered by prophets from Allah to guide humanity. Muslims believe in all prophets ending with Muhammad.

question_text: The first prophet in Islam according to Islamic tradition is:
explanation: Adam is considered the first prophet and the first human created by Allah. He received divine guidance and taught his descendants.

question_text: Which prophet is known as the 'Friend of Allah' (Khalilullah) in Islamic tradition?
explanation: Abraham is called Khalilullah (Friend of Allah) in Islamic tradition, reflecting his close relationship with God and his unwavering faith.

question_text: The prophet who was swallowed by a whale and repented to Allah is:
explanation: Prophet Yunus (Jonah) was swallowed by a large fish after leaving his people without Allah's permission. He repented from within the whale and was saved.

question_text: The revealed book given to Prophet Musa (Moses) is called:
explanation: The Tawrat (Torah) was revealed to Prophet Musa as guidance for the Children of Israel. Muslims believe it was later corrupted.

question_text: The Zabur (Psalms) was revealed to which prophet?
explanation: The Zabur was revealed to Prophet Dawud (David) as a book of divine wisdom and praises. It is mentioned in the Quran as a revelation from Allah.

question_text: The Injil (Gospel) was revealed to which prophet?
explanation: The Injil was revealed to Prophet Isa (Jesus) as guidance for the Children of Israel. Muslims believe the original Injil has been altered.

question_text: The Quran was revealed to Prophet Muhammad over approximately how many years?
explanation: The Quran was revealed progressively over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE when Muhammad was 40 and ending shortly before his death in 632 CE.

question_text: The first revelation received by Prophet Muhammad was:
explanation: The first revelation was the first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq (96:1-5), commanding 'Read in the name of your Lord who created.'

question_text: The number of chapters (Surahs) in the Holy Quran is:
explanation: The Quran consists of 114 chapters (Surahs), varying in length, revealed in Mecca and Medina over 23 years.

question_text: The longest chapter in the Quran is:
explanation: Surah Al-Baqarah is the longest chapter in the Quran with 286 verses, covering various aspects of Islamic law, faith, and guidance.

question_text: Surah Al-Fatiha is also known as:
option_a: The Opening and The Mother of the Book
explanation: Surah Al-Fatiha is called 'The Opening' because it opens the Quran and 'Umm al-Kitab' (Mother of the Book) due to its comprehensive praise and supplication.

question_text: Surah Al-Ikhlas emphasizes the concept of:
explanation: Surah Al-Ikhlas (112) powerfully affirms Tawhid, stating that Allah is One, Eternal, neither begetting nor begotten, and none is comparable to Him.

question_text: The Angel who delivered revelations to Prophet Muhammad is:
explanation: Jibreel (Gabriel) is the archangel responsible for conveying divine revelations to the prophets, including delivering the Quran to Muhammad.

question_text: The angel responsible for blowing the trumpet on the Day of Judgment is:
explanation: Israfil is the angel tasked with blowing the Sur (trumpet) to signal the coming of the Day of Judgment and the resurrection of the dead.

question_text: The angel of death in Islamic tradition is known as:
explanation: Azra'il (Malak al-Mawt) is the angel responsible for taking the souls of humans at the time of death.

question_text: The angels who record the deeds of humans are known as:
explanation: Kiraman Katibin (the noble scribes) are two angels assigned to every person, recording good and bad deeds respectively.

question_text: The term 'Yawm al-Qiyamah' refers to:
explanation: Yawm al-Qiyamah (Day of Resurrection or Judgment) is when all humanity will be raised from the dead and judged according to their deeds.

question_text: The bridge that all must cross on the Day of Judgment is called:
explanation: As-Sirat is the bridge over Hell that all must cross on Judgment Day. The righteous will cross quickly while sinners will fall into the fire below.

question_text: The scale used to weigh deeds on the Day of Judgment is called:
explanation: Al-Mizan is the divine scale that will weigh each person's good and bad deeds on the Day of Judgment to determine their fate.

question_text: The reservoir of the Prophet Muhammad on the Day of Judgment is known as:
explanation: Al-Hawd (or Kawthar) is the special pool or reservoir granted to Prophet Muhammad on the Day of Judgment, from which his followers will drink before entering Paradise.

question_text: The most authentic collection of Hadith after the Quran is:
explanation: Sahih al-Bukhari is considered the most authentic collection of Hadith, compiled by Imam Muhammad al-Bukhari over 16 years with rigorous criteria.

question_text: A Hadith Qudsi is defined as:
option_a: A divine saying where the meaning is from Allah but the wording from Muhammad
option_b: A saying about the Prophet's daily life
explanation: Hadith Qudsi (Sacred Hadith) contains divine revelation where Allah speaks through the Prophet Muhammad, but the words are the Prophet's, not part of the Quran.

question_text: The term 'Sunnah' in Islamic law refers to:
option_a: The practices and teachings of Prophet Muhammad
explanation: Sunnah encompasses the sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of Prophet Muhammad, serving as the second primary source of Islamic law after the Quran.

question_text: The chain of narrators in Hadith authentication is known as:
explanation: Isnad (or Sanad) refers to the chain of narrators who transmitted a Hadith, while Matn is the actual text. The chain's authenticity is critical for Hadith validation.

question_text: The five daily prayers in Islam are known as:
explanation: Salah (or Salat) refers to the five daily obligatory prayers performed by Muslims at specific times: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha.

question_text: The direction Muslims face during prayer is called:
explanation: Qibla is the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca that Muslims face during their prayers. The Qibla was changed from Jerusalem to Mecca during the Prophet's time.

question_text: The Friday congregational prayer is known as:
explanation: Salat al-Jumu'ah is the special Friday prayer that replaces the Dhuhr prayer, performed in congregation with a sermon (Khutbah).

question_text: The special night prayers performed during Ramadan are called:
explanation: Tarawih are special night prayers performed during Ramadan after Isha prayer, consisting of 8 or 20 rak'ahs, often with Quran recitation.

question_text: The pre-dawn voluntary prayer before Fajr is known as:
explanation: Tahajjud is the voluntary night prayer performed after waking from sleep, highly recommended in the Quran and Hadith.

question_text: The month of fasting in Islam is:
explanation: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar during which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, as prescribed in the Quran.

question_text: The meal eaten before dawn during Ramadan is called:
explanation: Suhur (or Suhoor) is the pre-dawn meal consumed before the fast begins at Fajr prayer. It is considered blessed and recommended by the Prophet.

question_text: The meal to break the fast at sunset is called:
explanation: Iftar is the evening meal breaking the daily fast at sunset, traditionally begun with dates and water following the Prophet's example.

question_text: The day on which fasting is prohibited (forbidden) is:
explanation: Fasting is forbidden on the two Eid days (Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha) as they are days of celebration and feasting.

question_text: Zakat is obligatory on wealth that has reached a certain minimum threshold called:
explanation: Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must possess before Zakat becomes due, calculated based on gold or silver value.

question_text: The percentage of Zakat due on most forms of wealth is:
explanation: The standard Zakat rate is 2.5% (1/40) of qualifying wealth that has been in one's possession for a full lunar year.

question_text: Voluntary charity given beyond obligatory Zakat is called:
explanation: Sadaqah refers to voluntary charity given out of goodwill and generosity, encouraged in Islam and can be monetary or through kind acts.

question_text: Zakat al-Fitr is due before which prayer?
explanation: Zakat al-Fitr (fitrana) must be paid before the Eid al-Fitr prayer to purify fasting imperfections and provide food for the needy.

question_text: The pilgrimage to Mecca that is obligatory once in a lifetime for those who can afford it is called:
explanation: Hajj is the major pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhul-Hijjah, one of the five pillars of Islam, obligatory once for those with physical and financial means.

question_text: The lesser pilgrimage that can be performed at any time of the year is called:
explanation: Umrah is the minor pilgrimage to Mecca that can be performed at any time of the year, involving Ihram, Tawaf, Sa'i, and shaving/trimming hair.

question_text: The ritual walking seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah during Hajj and Umrah commemorates:
option_a: Hagar's search for water for her son Ishmael
explanation: Sa'i reenacts Hagar's desperate search for water for her infant son Ishmael, after which the Zamzam well miraculously sprang forth.

question_text: The standing at Mount Arafat on the 9th of Dhul-Hijjah is known as:
explanation: Wuquf (standing) at Arafat is the most essential ritual of Hajj, without which Hajj is invalid. Pilgrims spend the afternoon in prayer and supplication.

question_text: The stoning of the pillars representing Satan at Mina is called:
explanation: Ramy al-Jamarat involves throwing seven pebbles at each of three pillars representing Satan, commemorating Abraham's rejection of Satan's temptations.

question_text: The migration of Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Medina is known as:
explanation: The Hijrah (migration) in 622 CE marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. It established the first Muslim community in Medina.

question_text: The night journey of Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem is called:
explanation: Isra refers to the Prophet's miraculous night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem (Al-Aqsa Mosque), mentioned in Surah Al-Isra (17:1).

question_text: The ascension of Prophet Muhammad through the heavens is called:
explanation: Mi'raj refers to the Prophet's ascension through the seven heavens to meet Allah and receive the obligation of five daily prayers.

question_text: The four rightly guided caliphs (Khulafa al-Rashidun) in order are:
explanation: The four rightly guided caliphs succeeded Prophet Muhammad in this order: Abu Bakr (632-634 CE), Umar (634-644 CE), Uthman (644-656 CE), and Ali (656-661 CE).

question_text: The compilation of the Quran into a single book format (mushaf) was ordered by which caliph?
explanation: After the Battle of Yamamah where many Quran memorizers died, Abu Bakr ordered Zaid ibn Thabit to compile the Quran into a single manuscript.

question_text: The standardization of the Quranic text and distribution to major cities was carried out by which caliph?
explanation: Caliph Uthman ordered the production of several standard copies of the Quran to unify the reading and sent them to major Islamic centers.

question_text: The first person to accept Islam among women was:
explanation: Khadijah, the wife of Prophet Muhammad, was the first woman and first person overall to accept Islam, providing crucial support.

question_text: The first person to accept Islam among men was:
explanation: Abu Bakr was the first adult male to accept Islam and became the Prophet's closest companion and first caliph.
